query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Explicit inclusion of oxygen-induced defect states via actively learned MLIPs will yield conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr across the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes that are within 50% of experimental measurements, thereby substantially reducing the overestimation (by roughly an order of magnitude) seen in ideal, defect‐free models.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk equimolar HfNbTaTiZr synthesized with a controlled oxygen contamination level of 1 wt.%, exhibiting intrinsic atomic inhomogeneities such as Ta-rich regions surrounded by Nb and segregated Ti, Zr, Hf, along with oxygen-induced oxide formations.
generation.intervention: Develop and deploy an actively learned MLIP trained on extensive datasets covering oxygen defect configurations at multiple temperatures. Use large-scale supercell simulations to explicitly model extended defects and non-ideal local chemical ordering, and tune scattering parameters for both low and high temperature regimes.
generation.conditions: Equilibrium simulation and measurement conditions spanning from cryogenic (0–200 K) to high-temperature (300–1200 K) regimes, ensuring the oxygen-doped microstructure is maintained.
generation.structural_mediator: Oxygen-related defect clusters and associated local chemical inhomogeneities, which alter electron scattering rates and influence effective relaxation times across the temperature spectrum.
generation.mechanism: The actively learned MLIP maps a broad configurational space that includes oxygen-induced defects, dynamically adjusting electronic relaxation parameters (such as relaxation time and effective plasma frequency) to account for enhanced scattering. This mechanism, validated across both low and high temperatures, significantly reduces conductivity overestimation compared to ideal models.
generation.predicted_outcome: Conductivity predictions across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K will match experimental values within 50% error, eliminating the approximately 10× overestimation observed with idealized approaches.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical and small-scale DFT models that assume perfect crystals, which overestimate conductivity by up to an order of magnitude.
generation.boundary: Applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with oxygen levels around 1 wt.% and for temperatures from nearly 0 K to 1200 K. At temperatures below 0 K, additional quantum effects might require further refinement.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty centers on the comprehensiveness of the MLIP training database for diverse oxygen defect configurations across temperatures. While the approach has strong support from MLIP advancements, incomplete sampling could lead to residual prediction errors.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform comprehensive conductivity measurements on bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with 1 wt.% oxygen across the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. Concurrently, use the developed MLIP-based framework to predict conductivity over these temperature ranges.
measurements: Low-frequency electrical conductivity measurements using four-point probe and terahertz spectroscopy at cryogenic and elevated temperatures.
Independent extraction of relaxation time and plasma frequency trends from experimental spectroscopic data.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP-based predicted conductivity values deviate by more than 50% from experimental measurements in any temperature regime, or if the reduction in overestimation compared to ideal models is not achieved, the hypothesis is falsified.

Another alternative to traditional supercell methods are machine-learning interatomic potentials (MLIPs) that are trained on ab initio data. The size of supercells is not limited with MLIPs, which is especially important when simulating extended defects like interfaces, where proper configurational averaging becomes an issue with MPEAs. In contrast to the previously proposed way of passively training general-purpose interatomic potentials on a pre-defined fixed training set (e.g.,,,), whose accuracy is not sufficient for our goals, especially for parts of the configurational space not covered by the training set, the use of active learning enables automatic generation of MLIP training sets specifically tailored to a given class of systems and a given set of properties. This allows one to predict any material property of interest with DFT accuracy over the entire composition space of an alloy, with a minimal amount of DFT calculations. papers.title: Microstructure and Room Temperature Mechanical Properties of Different 3 and 4 Element Medium Entropy Alloys from HfNbTaTiZr System.
papers.system: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr (5‐element system) and reduced-component derivatives
papers.approach: Ab‐initio Monte Carlo simulation to relax a 250‐atom BCC supercell at 300 K; experimental tensile and microstructure characterization
papers.findings: Simulations reveal pronounced atomic inhomogeneities (e.g. formation of one-dimensional Ta-rich ‘wire’ structures surrounded by Nb, with regions of Ti, Zr, Hf segregating) that may influence physical properties; experimentally, the 5-element HEA showed the best combination of strength and elongation compared to lower-element variants.
papers.mechanism: Local chemical inhomogeneity and segregation may lead to defect features that alter electronic scattering and transport compared with ideal, defect‐free crystals.

papers.title: The Effect of Processing Route on Properties of HfNbTaTiZr High Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr produced via powder metallurgy routes (including CIP, sintering, HIP, and spark plasma sintering)
papers.approach: Comparative processing routes with measurement of oxygen content, phase identification via XRD, and low-temperature positron lifetime studies
papers.findings: Samples prepared by mechanical alloying suffered from high oxygen levels (>1 wt%) leading to embrittlement, while spark plasma sintering of gas atomized powders yielded a single-phase, low-oxygen (~0.12 wt%) structure; oxygen content was correlated with hardness changes due to oxide particle formation.
papers.mechanism: Oxygen contamination promotes the formation of oxide particles (e.g., HfO2) and increases defect density, leading to modified mechanical (and possibly transport) properties versus ideal crystals.

papers.title: Ab initio framework for deciphering trade-off relationships in multi-component alloys.
papers.system: Refractory multi-principal element alloys including systems related to HfNbTaTiZr analogues
papers.approach: Combination of Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) and actively-learned Moment Tensor Potentials (MTPs) for large supercell simulations
papers.findings: The integrated method successfully captures extended defect effects (interfaces, dislocations) and predicts elastic constants, misfit volumes, and surface energies with DFT accuracy over a wide configuration space; demonstrates that conventional small supercell approaches (e.g., SQS) can produce errors on the order of 10–20% for surface energies.
papers.mechanism: Active learning MLIPs tailored to a given class of systems allow for interpolation within the defect-rich, non-ideal configurational space, thereby overcoming the limitations of assuming perfect crystal structures.

papers.title: Low-frequency conductivity of low wear high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Refractory HEAs (Nb-Mo-Ta-W system) with focus on conductivity modulation via elemental composition
papers.approach: Comparison of different estimation methods for conductivity – from the ideal solution (‘cocktail effect’) concept to ones incorporating plasma frequency and relaxation time effects – with experimental validation via terahertz spectroscopy
papers.findings: Ideal solution approaches overestimated conductivity by an order of magnitude, while methods that consider plasma frequency and relaxation time gave values within 50% error of experiment; this evidences that proper inclusion of microstructural defect effects (possibly relevant in oxygen-contaminated samples) is critical for accurate predictions.
papers.mechanism: Electronic scattering in HEAs is significantly altered by lattice distortions and defect states; hence, incorporating terms for plasma frequency and relaxation times (which are impacted by defects and chemical disorder) yields better predictive accuracy.

papers.title: Computational property predictions of Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: TaNbHfZr alloy, closely related to HfNbTaTiZr (sharing Hf, Nb, Ta, Zr with the addition of Ti in the latter)
papers.approach: Hybrid Monte Carlo/Molecular Dynamics simulations to evolve the nanostructure; dislocation simulations to predict yield strength; analysis of configurational entropy and local short-range order effects
papers.findings: Calculated properties such as yield strength and nanostructural evolution demonstrate that local chemical ordering and defect nucleation processes critically control mechanical (and by implication, transport) behavior; the simulation protocol captures both thermodynamic and kinetic aspects of defect evolution.
papers.mechanism: The interplay of configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and defect-induced scattering is critical in determining electronic transport and mechanical strength, offering a pathway to improved predictive methods when defects (e.g., oxygen contaminations) are present.

papers.title: Synergistic Strength-Ductility Improvement in an Additively Manufactured Body-Centered Cubic HfNbTaTiZr High-Entropy Alloy via Deep Cryogenic Treatment
papers.system: Additively manufactured HfNbTaTiZr designed for strength–ductility synergy, where deep cryogenic treatment influences residual stress and phase precipitation
papers.approach: Combined laser melting deposition (LMD) with deep cryogenic treatment (DCT) accompanied by finite element simulations and microstructural characterization
papers.findings: DCT induces significant residual stress changes and promotes stress-induced phase transitions (formation of Ti/Zr-rich HCP precipitates) that enhance both strength and ductility; these microstructural changes underscore the importance of defect and grain-boundary effects not captured in defect-free models.
papers.mechanism: Thermally driven defect nucleation and phase precipitation during rapid cooling and subsequent stress relaxation account for improved mechanical properties; by analogy, similar defect populations could influence conductivity.

directions.direction: Develop an actively learned machine‐learning interatomic potential (MLIP) framework that explicitly includes oxygen defect states and extended defect structures in large supercell simulations of bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
directions.assessment: Directly addresses the limitation of defect-free analytical predictions by explicitly modeling oxygen-induced defects and local chemical inhomogeneities. The physics of defect scattering and extended microstructural features is well established (e.g., via MLIP with active learning and CPA, see PMC11275555 and PMC11136967), and the approach has been demonstrated in related systems. It is computationally intensive but feasible and can deliver quantitative predictions of conductivity versus temperature.

directions.direction: Integrate Coherent Potential Approximation (CPA) with defect‐resolved MLIP simulations to correct the plasma frequency and relaxation time estimations in conductivity models for oxygen‐doped HfNbTaTiZr.
directions.assessment: This approach directly improves the analytical prediction by incorporating the effect of oxygen-induced scattering on electronic transport. It builds on prior evidence in HEAs that show the importance of relaxation time and plasma frequency corrections (PMC11136967, PMC11275555). The method respects the temperature ranges and sample constraints and is feasible with current computational techniques, providing a falsifiable benchmark prediction.

directions.direction: Implement a multi-scale simulation that couples atomistic defect modeling (using MLIPs/DFT) with mesoscale Monte Carlo simulations to capture defect clustering and phase segregation effects over temperature regimes.
directions.assessment: This strategy addresses both low (0–200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature regimes by capturing the evolution of defect states and oxide particle formation in oxygen‐contaminated HfNbTaTiZr. It leverages well‐known physics of defect clustering and extended inhomogeneity (as seen in PMC7514597 and PMC6926650) and could be highly informative if the overall conductivity predictions correlate with experimental measurements. The challenge is in coupling scales, but it remains feasible with current computational methods.

directions.direction: Use temperature‐dependent ab initio electronic structure calculations that incorporate explicit oxygen defect states and dynamic defect scattering effects to adjust relaxation times across the cryogenic and high-temperature regimes.
directions.assessment: By directly incorporating oxygen defect states into DFT-based methods and dynamically adjusting electron scattering parameters, this approach aims to predict conductivity trends over a wide temperature range. Supported by evidence of defect-induced scattering effects (PMC11136967, PMC6926650), this method overcomes the perfect crystal limitation and is falsifiable with a held-out benchmark. While computationally demanding, it is feasible and offers deep physical insight.

candidates.hypothesis: Explicit inclusion of oxygen-induced defect states via actively learned MLIPs will yield conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr across the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes that are within 50% of experimental measurements, thereby substantially reducing the overestimation (by roughly an order of magnitude) seen in ideal, defect‐free models.
candidates.intervention: Develop and deploy an actively learned MLIP trained on extensive datasets covering oxygen defect configurations at multiple temperatures. Use large-scale supercell simulations to explicitly model extended defects and non-ideal local chemical ordering, and tune scattering parameters for both low and high temperature regimes.
candidates.changes: Extended the original low-temperature-focused candidate to encompass the entire temperature range (0–200 K and 300–1200 K). Detailed the plan to train MLIPs on datasets including oxygen-induced defect states across temperature regimes and clarified the mechanism by which the MLIP adjusts scattering parameters.

minor_issues: Further details on how quantum corrections are integrated with MLIP predictions at very low temperatures would strengthen the mechanism.
The approach could clarify how oxide evolution under high-temperature exposure is managed to ensure microstructural stability.
fixes: Add more specifics about implementing quantum corrections and validating them with known low-temperature data.
Provide an explicit plan for tracking any microstructural changes due to further oxidation at high temperatures.
evidence_needs: Experimental references on temperature-dependent electron-defect scattering in oxygen-bearing high-entropy alloys to confirm the planned coupling of DFT with MLIPs.
Prior results demonstrating synergy between ab initio calculations and active learning for defect-rich alloy systems.
